## Introduction to Belt and Pulley Systems {#sec-belts-intro}

Belt and pulley systems represent one of the oldest and most versatile methods of mechanical power transmission. From the spinning wheels of ancient civilizations to modern automotive engines and industrial machinery, belts have been transmitting power across distances for thousands of years.

> **Think About It:** Look around your everyday environment. Your car uses multiple belt drives—the serpentine belt powers the alternator, water pump, and air conditioning compressor. A drill press uses belts to change speeds. Even household appliances like washing machines and vacuum cleaners rely on belt drives. Why do engineers choose belts over direct gear connections in so many applications?

The answer lies in the unique advantages belt drives offer:

- **Shock absorption** – Belts naturally dampen vibrations and load spikes
- **Distance** – Power can be transmitted over relatively long center distances
- **Speed flexibility** – Easy to change speed ratios by swapping pulleys
- **Quiet operation** – Much quieter than gear or chain drives
- **Overload protection** – Belts slip before catastrophic failure occurs
- **Low cost** – Generally less expensive than gear systems

## Fundamental Belt Drive Concepts {#sec-belt-fundamentals}

### How Belt Drives Work

A belt drive consists of at least two pulleys connected by a flexible belt. When the driving pulley (connected to the motor or power source) rotates, friction between the belt and pulley surface transmits the motion to the driven pulley.

```{r belt-drive-diagram, echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', fig.cap="Basic two-pulley open belt drive. The driver turns counter-clockwise and pulls the belt in from the upper span, so the upper span is the tight side and the lower span the slack side.", fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
library(ggplot2)
## ---- Belt path through a list of pulleys --------------------------------------------
## Pulleys are visited in the order the belt travels (counter-clockwise loop).
## sigma = +1: pulley inside the loop (belt wraps it CCW); -1: outside (backside idler, wrapped CW).
belt_path <- function(P) {
  n <- nrow(P); seg <- list(); tp <- vector("list", n)
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    j <- i %% n + 1
    D <- c(P$x[j] - P$x[i], P$y[j] - P$y[i]); L <- sqrt(sum(D^2)); phi <- atan2(D[2], D[1])
    g <- acos((P$s[i] * P$r[i] - P$s[j] * P$r[j]) / L)
    nrm <- c(cos(phi - g), sin(phi - g))                       # right-hand normal of the span
    pi_ <- c(P$x[i], P$y[i]) + P$s[i] * P$r[i] * nrm
    pj_ <- c(P$x[j], P$y[j]) + P$s[j] * P$r[j] * nrm
    seg[[i]] <- data.frame(x = c(pi_[1], pj_[1]), y = c(pi_[2], pj_[2]))
    tp[[i]]$out <- pi_; tp[[j]]$inn <- pj_
  }
  arcs <- lapply(seq_len(n), function(k) {
    a1 <- atan2(tp[[k]]$inn[2] - P$y[k], tp[[k]]$inn[1] - P$x[k])
    a2 <- atan2(tp[[k]]$out[2] - P$y[k], tp[[k]]$out[1] - P$x[k])
    if (P$s[k] > 0) { while (a2 < a1) a2 <- a2 + 2 * pi } else { while (a2 > a1) a2 <- a2 - 2 * pi }
    t <- seq(a1, a2, length.out = 60)
    data.frame(x = P$x[k] + P$r[k] * cos(t), y = P$y[k] + P$r[k] * sin(t), wrap = abs(a2 - a1))
  })
  list(spans = seg, arcs = arcs)
}
disc <- function(x, y, r, n = 120) { t <- seq(0, 2 * pi, length.out = n); data.frame(x = x + r * cos(t), y = y + r * sin(t)) }
rot_arc <- function(x, y, r, from, to, col) {
  t <- seq(from, to, length.out = 30) * pi / 180
  annotate("path", x = x + r * cos(t), y = y + r * sin(t), color = col, linewidth = 1.1,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"), type = "closed"))
}

P <- data.frame(x = c(0, 8), y = c(0, 0), r = c(1.5, 3), s = c(1, 1))
bp <- belt_path(P)
wrap1 <- bp$arcs[[1]]$wrap[1] * 180 / pi

ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = disc(0, 0, 1.5), aes(x, y), fill = "steelblue", color = "darkblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_polygon(data = disc(0, 0, 0.45), aes(x, y), fill = "gray30", color = "black") +
  geom_polygon(data = disc(8, 0, 3), aes(x, y), fill = "coral", color = "darkred", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_polygon(data = disc(8, 0, 0.45), aes(x, y), fill = "gray30", color = "black") +
  geom_path(data = bp$arcs[[1]], aes(x, y), linewidth = 2.5, color = "gray15") +
  geom_path(data = bp$arcs[[2]], aes(x, y), linewidth = 2.5, color = "gray15") +
  geom_path(data = bp$spans[[1]], aes(x, y), linewidth = 2.5, color = "gray50") +      # lower span (slack)
  geom_path(data = bp$spans[[2]], aes(x, y), linewidth = 2.5, color = "black") +       # upper span (tight)
  rot_arc(0, 0, 2.1, 20, 110, "darkblue") + rot_arc(8, 0, 3.6, 30, 80, "darkred") +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = -2.6, label = "Driver Pulley\n(Small, Fast)", size = 4 * diagram_text_scale, fontface = "bold", color = "darkblue") +
  annotate("text", x = 8, y = -4.1, label = "Driven Pulley\n(Large, Slow)", size = 4 * diagram_text_scale, fontface = "bold", color = "darkred") +
  annotate("text", x = 4, y = 3.5, label = "Tight Side (High Tension T1)", size = 3.5 * diagram_text_scale) +
  annotate("text", x = 4, y = -3.4, label = "Slack Side (Low Tension T2)", size = 3.5 * diagram_text_scale, color = "gray40") +
  annotate("text", x = -1.9, y = 1.4, label = sprintf("wrap %.0f°", wrap1), size = 3.2 * diagram_text_scale, color = "darkblue", hjust = 1) +
  annotate("segment", x = 0, y = -5.2, xend = 8, yend = -5.2, arrow = arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(0.2, "cm")), color = "darkgreen") +
  annotate("text", x = 4, y = -5.7, label = "Center Distance (C)", size = 4 * diagram_text_scale, color = "darkgreen", fontface = "italic") +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(-3.5, 11.5), ylim = c(-6, 4.2)) +
  theme_pulley +
  labs(title = "Open Belt Drive System",
       subtitle = "Speed reduction: the large driven pulley turns slower and with more torque")
```

### The Speed Ratio

The fundamental relationship in any belt drive is the **speed ratio** (also called the velocity ratio). Since the belt travels at a constant linear velocity around both pulleys:

$$v_{belt} = \omega_1 \times r_1 = \omega_2 \times r_2$$

This leads to the fundamental speed ratio equation:

$$\frac{n_2}{n_1} = \frac{D_1}{D_2} = \frac{1}{i}$$

Where:

| Symbol | Description | Unit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $n_1$ | Rotational speed of driver pulley | rpm |
| $n_2$ | Rotational speed of driven pulley | rpm |
| $D_1$ | Pitch diameter of driver pulley | mm or in |
| $D_2$ | Pitch diameter of driven pulley | mm or in |
| $i$ | Speed ratio (transmission ratio) | dimensionless |

> **Key Insight:** When the driver pulley is smaller than the driven pulley, the output speed decreases but the output torque increases proportionally. This is the principle of **mechanical advantage** applied to rotational systems.

## Essential Belt Drive Terminology {#sec-belt-terminology}

Understanding belt drive terminology is essential for proper selection and design.

```{r pulley-terminology, echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', fig.cap="Half-section of a V-belt pulley (sheave) through its axis, with the belt seated in the groove. The belt wedges against the groove walls and does not touch the bottom of the groove.", fig.width=8, fig.height=7}
library(ggplot2)
tb <- tan(19 * pi / 180)                    # groove half-angle 19 deg (38 deg groove)
hw <- function(y) 0.24 + (y - 3.1) * tb      # groove half-width at height y
rim <- data.frame(x = c(-1.4, 1.4, 1.4, hw(4), hw(3.1), -hw(3.1), -hw(4), -1.4),
                  y = c(3.0, 3.0, 4.0, 4.0, 3.1, 3.1, 4.0, 4.0))
belt <- data.frame(x = c(-hw(4.15), hw(4.15), hw(3.55), -hw(3.55)), y = c(4.15, 4.15, 3.55, 3.55))
apex_y <- 3.1 - 0.24 / tb
ggplot() +
  annotate("segment", x = -2.6, xend = 2.6, y = 0, yend = 0, linetype = "F282", color = "red") +
  annotate("text", x = 2.7, y = 0, label = "axis of rotation", hjust = 0, color = "red", size = 3 * diagram_text_scale) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -1.6, xmax = 1.6, ymin = 0.6, ymax = 1.4, fill = "gray70", color = "black") +    # hub
  annotate("rect", xmin = -0.35, xmax = 0.35, ymin = 1.4, ymax = 3.0, fill = "gray70", color = "black") +  # web
  geom_polygon(data = rim, aes(x, y), fill = "gray70", color = "black") +                                  # rim with groove
  geom_polygon(data = belt, aes(x, y), fill = "gray15", color = "black") +
  ## groove angle: walls extended to their apex
  annotate("segment", x = c(-hw(3.1), hw(3.1)), xend = 0, y = 3.1, yend = apex_y, linetype = "dashed", color = "blue") +
  annotate("path", x = 0.45 * sin(seq(-19, 19, length.out = 20) * pi / 180), y = apex_y + 0.45 * cos(seq(-19, 19, length.out = 20) * pi / 180), color = "blue") +
  annotate("text", x = -1.0, y = 2.55, label = "Groove angle β\n(34–38°)", color = "blue", size = 3.2 * diagram_text_scale, hjust = 1) +
  annotate("segment", x = -0.98, xend = -0.1, y = 2.6, yend = apex_y + 0.4, color = "blue", linewidth = 0.3) +
  ## groove depth
  annotate("segment", x = 1.75, xend = 1.75, y = 3.1, yend = 4.0, arrow = arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(0.12, "cm")), color = "purple") +
  annotate("segment", x = hw(3.1), xend = 1.85, y = 3.1, yend = 3.1, color = "purple", linewidth = 0.3, linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("text", x = 1.9, y = 3.55, label = "Groove depth", hjust = 0, color = "purple", size = 3.2 * diagram_text_scale) +
  ## pitch radius: axis to the belt's pitch line
  annotate("segment", x = -hw(3.95) - 0.8, xend = hw(3.95) + 0.1, y = 3.95, yend = 3.95, linetype = "dashed", color = "darkgreen", linewidth = 0.4) +
  annotate("segment", x = -2.2, xend = -2.2, y = 0, yend = 3.95, arrow = arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(0.15, "cm")), color = "darkgreen") +
  annotate("text", x = -2.3, y = 2.0, label = "Pitch\nradius", hjust = 1, color = "darkgreen", size = 3.2 * diagram_text_scale) +
  annotate("text", x = 0, y = 4.45, label = "V-belt", fontface = "bold", size = 4 * diagram_text_scale) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.6, y = 3.32, label = "gap", size = 2.6 * diagram_text_scale, color = "gray30", hjust = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.9, y = 1.0, label = "Hub (bore for\nshaft below)", hjust = 0, size = 3 * diagram_text_scale) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.5, y = 2.2, label = "Web", hjust = 0, size = 3 * diagram_text_scale) +
  annotate("text", x = 1.55, y = 4.25, label = "Rim", hjust = 0, size = 3 * diagram_text_scale) +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(-3.6, 4.2), ylim = c(-0.3, 4.7)) +
  theme_pulley +
  labs(title = "V-Belt Pulley Half-Section",
       subtitle = "The belt rides on the groove walls, not the bottom")
```

### Key Terminology Table

| Term | Definition |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Pulley (Sheave)** | The rotating wheel with a grooved rim that guides and grips the belt |
| **Pitch Diameter** | The effective diameter where the belt's neutral axis contacts the pulley |
| **Outside Diameter** | The largest diameter of the pulley (top of flanges) |
| **Groove Angle** | The angle of the V-groove, typically 34° to 40° |
| **Center Distance** | The distance between the shaft centers of driver and driven pulleys |
| **Belt Span** | The unsupported length of belt between pulleys |
| **Tight Side** | The belt span under higher tension (pulling side) |
| **Slack Side** | The belt span under lower tension (returning side) |
| **Arc of Contact** | The angle through which the belt wraps around a pulley |
| **Belt Pitch Length** | The total length measured at the belt's neutral axis |
| **Creep** | Slight slippage between belt and pulley due to elastic stretch |
| **Slip** | Relative motion between belt and pulley surfaces (undesirable) |

## Types of Belts {#sec-belt-types}

Different applications require different belt types. Each has distinct characteristics that make it suitable for specific uses.

### V-Belts

V-belts are the most common type of power transmission belt. Their trapezoidal cross-section wedges into the pulley groove, creating a friction grip that increases with load.

```{r v-belt-profile, echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', fig.cap="V-belt cross-section profiles for different standard sizes", fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
## Create V-belt cross-section comparison
library(ggplot2)

## Function to create V-belt profile
create_vbelt <- function(width_top, width_bottom, height, x_offset, label) {
  data.frame(
    x = c(x_offset - width_top/2, x_offset - width_bottom/2,
          x_offset + width_bottom/2, x_offset + width_top/2),
    y = c(height, 0, 0, height),
    label = label
  )
}

## Standard V-belt sizes (approximate proportions)
belt_A <- create_vbelt(0.5, 0.3, 0.31, 0, "A")
belt_B <- create_vbelt(0.66, 0.4, 0.41, 1.5, "B")
belt_C <- create_vbelt(0.88, 0.53, 0.53, 3.2, "C")
belt_D <- create_vbelt(1.25, 0.75, 0.75, 5.2, "D")
belt_E <- create_vbelt(1.5, 0.91, 0.91, 7.5, "E")

## Combine all belts
all_belts <- rbind(belt_A, belt_B, belt_C, belt_D, belt_E)

## Create specifications table data
specs <- data.frame(
  label = c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E"),
  x_pos = c(0, 1.5, 3.2, 5.2, 7.5),
  top_width = c("1/2\"", "21/32\"", "7/8\"", "1-1/4\"", "1-1/2\""),
  height = c("5/16\"", "13/32\"", "17/32\"", "3/4\"", "29/32\""),
  hp_range = c("0.5-10", "1-25", "15-100", "50-250", "100-500")
)

ggplot() +
  ## Draw each belt profile
  geom_polygon(data = belt_A, aes(x = x, y = y), fill = "gray20", color = "black") +
  geom_polygon(data = belt_B, aes(x = x, y = y), fill = "gray25", color = "black") +
  geom_polygon(data = belt_C, aes(x = x, y = y), fill = "gray30", color = "black") +
  geom_polygon(data = belt_D, aes(x = x, y = y), fill = "gray35", color = "black") +
  geom_polygon(data = belt_E, aes(x = x, y = y), fill = "gray40", color = "black") +
  ## Labels
  geom_text(data = specs, aes(x = x_pos, y = -0.3, label = label),
            size = 6 * diagram_text_scale, fontface = "bold", color = "darkblue") +
  ## Dimension annotations
  geom_text(data = specs, aes(x = x_pos, y = -0.55,
                              label = paste0("Top: ", top_width)),
            size = 3 * diagram_text_scale, color = "gray40") +
  geom_text(data = specs, aes(x = x_pos, y = -0.75,
                              label = paste0("H: ", height)),
            size = 3 * diagram_text_scale, color = "gray40") +
  geom_text(data = specs, aes(x = x_pos, y = -0.95,
                              label = paste0(hp_range, " HP")),
            size = 3 * diagram_text_scale, color = "darkgreen") +
  coord_fixed() +
  xlim(-1, 9) +
  ylim(-1.2, 1.2) +
  theme_pulley +
  labs(title = "Standard V-Belt Cross-Section Sizes",
       subtitle = "Classical V-belt profiles (A through E) showing relative sizes and typical power ranges")
```

**V-Belt Advantages:**

- High friction grip due to wedging action
- Quiet operation
- Absorbs shock loads
- Slips before failure (overload protection)
- Inexpensive and widely available

**V-Belt Limitations:**

- Some slip and creep (typically 1-2%)
- Not suitable for precise timing applications
- Limited speed ratio (typically up to 6:1)
- Temperature sensitive

### Timing Belts (Synchronous Belts)

Timing belts have teeth that mesh with grooves in the pulley, providing positive engagement without slip. They are essential when precise speed ratios and synchronized motion are required.

```{r timing-belt-diagram, echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', fig.cap="Timing belt teeth meshing with the grooves of a timing pulley (shown developed into a straight rack for clarity). The pitch is measured along the pitch line, which lies in the tension cords of the belt.", fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
library(ggplot2)
p <- 1; n <- 8; tw_root <- 0.62; tw_tip <- 0.42; th <- 0.38; back <- 0.45
## belt teeth hang down from the backing; pulley grooves have the same shape plus a small clearance
tooth <- function(i, w1, w2, h, y0, id) data.frame(x = i * p + c(-w1, w1, w2, -w2) / 2, y = y0 - c(0, 0, h, h), id = id)
teeth <- do.call(rbind, lapply(0:(n - 1), function(i) tooth(i, tw_root, tw_tip, th, 0, i)))
grooves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(0:(n - 1), function(i) tooth(i, tw_root + 0.06, tw_tip + 0.06, th + 0.05, 0, i)))
ggplot() +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -0.7, xmax = n - 0.3, ymin = -1.2, ymax = 0, fill = "gray75", color = "black") +   # pulley rim
  geom_polygon(data = grooves, aes(x, y, group = id), fill = "white", color = "black", linewidth = 0.4) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -0.7, xmax = n - 0.3, ymin = 0, ymax = back, fill = "gray30", color = "black") +   # belt backing
  geom_polygon(data = teeth, aes(x, y, group = id), fill = "gray30", color = "black", linewidth = 0.4) +
  annotate("segment", x = -0.7, xend = n - 0.3, y = 0.12, yend = 0.12, color = "gold", linewidth = 1.2) +    # tension cords / pitch line
  annotate("segment", x = 1, xend = 2, y = 0.75, yend = 0.75, arrow = arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(0.15, "cm")), color = "darkgreen") +
  annotate("segment", x = c(1, 2), xend = c(1, 2), y = 0.12, yend = 0.85, color = "darkgreen", linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = 0.98, label = "Pitch p", color = "darkgreen", size = 3.5 * diagram_text_scale) +
  annotate("text", x = n - 0.1, y = 0.12, label = "Pitch line\n(tension cords)", hjust = 0, color = "goldenrod4", size = 3 * diagram_text_scale) +
  annotate("segment", x = -1.0, xend = -1.0, y = 0, yend = -th, arrow = arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(0.1, "cm")), color = "purple") +
  annotate("text", x = -1.1, y = -th / 2, label = "Tooth\nheight", hjust = 1, color = "purple", size = 3 * diagram_text_scale) +
  annotate("segment", x = -1.0, xend = -1.0, y = 0, yend = back, arrow = arrow(ends = "both", length = unit(0.1, "cm")), color = "blue") +
  annotate("text", x = -1.1, y = back / 2 + 0.05, label = "Backing", hjust = 1, color = "blue", size = 3 * diagram_text_scale) +
  annotate("text", x = (n - 1) / 2, y = 1.35, label = "Timing Belt (Toothed Belt)", size = 5 * diagram_text_scale, fontface = "bold") +
  annotate("text", x = (n - 1) / 2, y = -1.5, label = "Timing Pulley (developed)", size = 4 * diagram_text_scale, fontface = "bold", color = "gray40") +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(-2.4, n + 1.3), ylim = c(-1.8, 1.6)) +
  theme_pulley
```

**Timing Belt Advantages:**

- No slip – exact speed ratio maintained
- Can transmit high torque
- Suitable for precision positioning
- Long service life with proper maintenance
- No lubrication required

**Timing Belt Applications:**

- Automotive camshaft drives (hence "timing belt")
- CNC machines and 3D printers
- Robotics and automation
- Conveyor systems requiring precise indexing

### Flat Belts

Flat belts are the simplest type, consisting of a rectangular cross-section. Modern flat belts often have a high-friction coating and can handle very high speeds.

**Flat Belt Characteristics:**

| Property | Rating |
| :--- | :--- |
| Speed capability | Excellent (up to 50 m/s) |
| Power capacity | Moderate |
| Efficiency | Very high (98%+) |
| Noise | Very quiet |
| Cost | Low |
| Typical use | Light-duty, high-speed applications |

### Ribbed (Poly-V) Belts

Ribbed belts combine the high-speed capability of flat belts with the grip of V-belts. Multiple small V-ribs run along the belt's inner surface.

```{r belt-comparison-table, echo=FALSE}
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)

comparison_df <- data.frame(
  Feature = c("Slip/Creep", "Speed Ratio Accuracy", "Maximum Speed",

              "Typical Applications"),

               "HVAC, pumps, compressors"),

                    "Automotive engines, CNC, robotics"),

                  "High-speed machinery, textiles"),
  `Ribbed Belt` = c("<1%", "Very Good", "40 m/s", "Good", "Low", "Moderate", "Low",
                    "Automotive accessories, appliances"),

      caption = "Comparison of Belt Types",
      align = c('l', 'c', 'c', 'c', 'c')) %>%
  kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed"),

## Belt Drive Calculations {#sec-belt-calculations}

### Speed Ratio and Output Speed

The speed ratio is the fundamental calculation for any belt drive system:

$$i = \frac{n_1}{n_2} = \frac{D_2}{D_1}$$

Rearranging to find the output speed:

$$n_2 = n_1 \times \frac{D_1}{D_2}$$

> **Example:** A motor running at 1750 rpm drives a 100 mm pulley. The driven pulley is 250 mm. What is the output speed?
>
> $$n_2 = 1750 \times \frac{100}{250} = 700 \text{ rpm}$$

### Belt Length Calculation

For an open belt drive (the most common configuration), the required belt pitch length is:

$$L = 2C + \frac{\pi}{2}(D_1 + D_2) + \frac{(D_2 - D_1)^2}{4C}$$

Where:

| Symbol | Description | Unit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $L$ | Belt pitch length | mm |
| $C$ | Center distance between pulleys | mm |
| $D_1$ | Pitch diameter of smaller pulley | mm |
| $D_2$ | Pitch diameter of larger pulley | mm |

### Center Distance from Belt Length

If you have a standard belt length and need to calculate the center distance:

$$C = \frac{B + \sqrt{B^2 - 8(D_2 - D_1)^2}}{8}$$

Where:

$$B = 2L - \pi(D_1 + D_2)$$

### Arc of Contact

The arc of contact (wrap angle) on the smaller pulley is critical for power transmission:

$$\theta_1 = 180° - 2\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{D_2 - D_1}{2C}\right)$$

> **Design Rule:** The arc of contact on the smaller pulley should be at least 120° for adequate grip. Values below this require adjustment of center distance or use of an idler pulley.

### Belt Speed

The linear belt speed affects both power capacity and belt life:

$$v = \frac{\pi \times D \times n}{60,000}$$

Where:

| Symbol | Description | Unit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $v$ | Belt linear velocity | m/s |
| $D$ | Pulley pitch diameter | mm |
| $n$ | Rotational speed | rpm |

> **Design Rule:** For V-belts, optimal belt speed is typically 15-25 m/s. Speeds above 30 m/s cause excessive centrifugal force and reduce belt grip.

### Power Transmission

The power transmitted by a belt drive depends on the tension difference between tight and slack sides:

$$P = (T_1 - T_2) \times v$$

Where:

| Symbol | Description | Unit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $P$ | Power transmitted | W |
| $T_1$ | Tight side tension | N |
| $T_2$ | Slack side tension | N |
| $v$ | Belt velocity | m/s |

The tension ratio is governed by the friction equation:

$$\frac{T_1}{T_2} = e^{\mu\theta}$$

Where $\mu$ is the coefficient of friction between belt and pulley, and $\theta$ is the arc of contact in radians.

---

## 🧮 Worked Example: Belt Drive Design {-}

**Problem:** Design a V-belt drive system to transmit 5 kW from a 1450 rpm electric motor to a machine shaft that must rotate at approximately 500 rpm. The center distance should be approximately 500 mm.

<details>
<summary>**Click to reveal solution**</summary>

**Step 1: Calculate the required speed ratio**

$$i = \frac{n_1}{n_2} = \frac{1450}{500} = 2.9$$

**Step 2: Select pulley diameters**

Choose a driver pulley diameter (standard sizes: 75, 90, 100, 112, 125, 140, 160 mm...)

Let's select $D_1 = 100$ mm

Then: $D_2 = D_1 \times i = 100 \times 2.9 = 290$ mm

Select nearest standard size: $D_2 = 280$ mm (or 315 mm)

With $D_2 = 280$ mm, actual speed ratio: $i = 280/100 = 2.8$

Actual output speed: $n_2 = 1450/2.8 = 518$ rpm ✓ (close to target)

**Step 3: Calculate belt length**

$$L = 2(500) + \frac{\pi}{2}(100 + 280) + \frac{(280 - 100)^2}{4(500)}$$

$$L = 1000 + 596.9 + 16.2 = 1613.1 \text{ mm}$$

Classical V-belts are designated by their *inside* length in inches; for B-section belts the pitch length is about 1.8 in longer. The required pitch length, 1613 mm = 63.5 in, corresponds to an inside length of 61.7 in, so select **B62** (pitch length about 63.8 in = 1621 mm). With $L = 1621$ mm the center-distance formula gives $C = 504$ mm, close to the 500 mm target.

**Step 4: Verify arc of contact**

$$\theta_1 = 180° - 2\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{280 - 100}{2 \times 500}\right)$$

$$\theta_1 = 180° - 2\sin^{-1}(0.18) = 180° - 20.7° = 159.3°$$

This exceeds 120°, so grip is adequate. ✓

**Step 5: Check belt speed**

$$v = \frac{\pi \times 100 \times 1450}{60,000} = 7.6 \text{ m/s}$$

This is well below the 15-25 m/s optimum. It is acceptable (V-belts work down to about 5 m/s), but at this low speed each belt transmits less power, so more belts or a larger driver pulley may be needed. A 140 mm driver with a 400 mm driven pulley (ratio 2.86) would run the belt at 10.6 m/s.

**Step 6: Select belt cross-section**

For 5 kW at 1450 rpm with a 100 mm pulley, referencing V-belt power rating tables, a **B-section** V-belt is appropriate. One belt should be sufficient, but two belts would provide a safety factor.

**Summary:**

- Driver pulley: 100 mm pitch diameter, B-section groove
- Driven pulley: 280 mm pitch diameter, B-section groove
- Belt: B62 (about 1621 mm pitch length), B-section
- Center distance: about 504 mm (adjustable motor base for tensioning)
- Output speed: 518 rpm

</details>

---

## ⚡ Belt Tensioning {-}

Proper belt tension is critical for reliable operation. Too little tension causes slip and rapid wear; too much tension damages bearings and shortens belt life.

### Tension Guidelines

| Belt Type | Tension Check Method | Acceptable Deflection |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| V-Belt | Force-deflection method | Deflection of 1/64 of the span length (about 1.6 %) under the specified test force |
| Timing Belt | Frequency measurement | Specified Hz range |
| Flat Belt | Visual/manual check | Minimal visible sag |

### Tensioning Methods

1. **Adjustable motor base** – Motor slides to adjust center distance
2. **Idler pulley** – Additional pulley presses against slack side
3. **Automatic tensioner** – Spring-loaded pulley maintains constant tension
4. **Screw adjustment** – Threaded adjustment for precise tension setting

```{r idler-pulley-diagram, echo=FALSE, fig.align='center', fig.cap="Belt drive with a backside idler tensioner. The spring-loaded idler presses on the back of the slack span from outside the loop, which also increases the wrap on both pulleys.", fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
library(ggplot2)
P <- data.frame(x = c(0, 3.4, 8), y = c(0, -1.25, 0), r = c(1.2, 0.6, 2.5), s = c(1, -1, 1))
bp <- belt_path(P)
ggplot() +
  geom_polygon(data = disc(0, 0, 1.2), aes(x, y), fill = "steelblue", color = "darkblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_polygon(data = disc(8, 0, 2.5), aes(x, y), fill = "coral", color = "darkred", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_polygon(data = disc(3.4, -1.25, 0.6), aes(x, y), fill = "gold", color = "darkorange", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_polygon(data = rbind(disc(0, 0, 0.3), disc(8, 0, 0.3), disc(3.4, -1.25, 0.18)) |> transform(g = rep(1:3, each = 120)),
               aes(x, y, group = g), fill = "gray30", color = "black") +
  lapply(bp$arcs, function(a) geom_path(data = a, aes(x, y), linewidth = 2.5, color = "gray15")) +
  geom_path(data = bp$spans[[3]], aes(x, y), linewidth = 2.5, color = "black") +
  geom_path(data = bp$spans[[1]], aes(x, y), linewidth = 2.5, color = "gray50") +
  geom_path(data = bp$spans[[2]], aes(x, y), linewidth = 2.5, color = "gray50") +
  rot_arc(0, 0, 1.8, 30, 120, "darkblue") +
  annotate("segment", x = 3.4, y = -3.0, xend = 3.4, yend = -2.0, color = "darkgreen", linewidth = 1.5,
           arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.25, "cm"), type = "closed")) +
  annotate("text", x = 3.4, y = -3.4, label = "Spring force", size = 3.5 * diagram_text_scale, color = "darkgreen") +
  annotate("text", x = -1.9, y = 1.6, label = "Driver", size = 4 * diagram_text_scale, fontface = "bold", color = "darkblue") +
  annotate("text", x = 8, y = 3.1, label = "Driven", size = 4 * diagram_text_scale, fontface = "bold", color = "darkred") +
  annotate("text", x = 4.4, y = -2.5, label = "Backside idler\n(on the slack side)", hjust = 0, size = 3.5 * diagram_text_scale, fontface = "bold", color = "darkorange") +
  annotate("text", x = 4, y = 2.3, label = "Tight side", size = 3.5 * diagram_text_scale) +
  coord_fixed(xlim = c(-2.5, 11.5), ylim = c(-4.8, 3.6)) +
  theme_pulley +
  labs(title = "Belt Drive with Automatic Tensioner",
       subtitle = "A spring-loaded idler on the slack side keeps the belt tension constant")
```

## 🎯 Design Guidelines and Best Practices {-}

### Pulley Selection Guidelines

| Parameter | Recommendation |
| :--- | :--- |
| Minimum pulley diameter | Follow belt manufacturer specifications |
| Speed ratio | Keep below 6:1 for single-stage drives |
| Number of belts | Use multiple belts for high power or redundancy |
| Material | Cast iron or steel for most applications; aluminum for light duty |
| Groove angle | Set by pulley size: about 34° on small-diameter pulleys, up to 38° on large ones (the belt section narrows as it bends) |

### Installation Best Practices

1. **Alignment** – Pulleys must be parallel and in the same plane
2. **Tension** – Set initial tension per manufacturer specifications
3. **Run-in period** – Re-tension after 24-48 hours of operation
4. **Inspection** – Check belt condition and tension regularly
5. **Replacement** – Replace all belts in a multi-belt drive together

### Common Problems and Solutions

| Problem | Likely Cause | Solution |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Belt squeal | Insufficient tension or contamination | Increase tension; clean pulleys |
| Rapid wear | Misalignment or wrong belt size | Realign pulleys; verify belt selection |
| Belt slipping | Worn belt or low tension | Replace belt; adjust tension |
| Overheating | Excessive slip or overload | Reduce load; check alignment |
| Belt cracking | Age, heat, or chemical exposure | Replace belt; protect from environment |

## 📚 Chapter Summary {-}

Belt and pulley systems provide a versatile, economical method for transmitting rotational power. Key takeaways:

1. **Speed ratio** is determined by the ratio of pulley diameters: $i = D_2/D_1$

2. **V-belts** are most common for general power transmission; **timing belts** for precise synchronization

3. **Belt length** calculation considers center distance and both pulley diameters

4. **Arc of contact** must exceed 120° on the smaller pulley for reliable grip

5. **Proper tensioning** is critical – not too tight, not too loose

6. **Belt speed** affects both power capacity and service life

## Try it yourself {#sec-belt-tryit}

These use drives that are not in the worked example. Each exercise checks your answer and lets you try again.

### Belt length, arc of contact and belt speed {#sec-tryit-belt-grid}

```{r tryit-belt-grid, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
bd <- data.frame(
  `Drive` = c("Fan drive", "Pump drive", "Compact drive"),
  `D1 (mm)` = c(90, 125, 63),
  `D2 (mm)` = c(280, 315, 400),
  `C (mm)` = c(450, 600, 300),
  `n1 (rpm)` = c(1440, 1750, 960),
  check.names = FALSE
)
bd[["Belt length L (mm)"]]      <- 2 * bd[["C (mm)"]] + pi / 2 * (bd[["D1 (mm)"]] + bd[["D2 (mm)"]]) +
                                    (bd[["D2 (mm)"]] - bd[["D1 (mm)"]])^2 / (4 * bd[["C (mm)"]])
bd[["Arc of contact (deg)"]]    <- 180 - 2 * asin((bd[["D2 (mm)"]] - bd[["D1 (mm)"]]) / (2 * bd[["C (mm)"]])) * 180 / pi
bd[["Belt speed (m/s)"]]        <- pi * bd[["D1 (mm)"]] * bd[["n1 (rpm)"]] / 60000
bd_n_fail <- sum(bd[["Arc of contact (deg)"]] < 120)

tryit_grid(
  id = "belt-grid",
  title = "Three belt drives",
  data = bd,
  blank = c("Belt length L (mm)", "Arc of contact (deg)", "Belt speed (m/s)"),
  tol = c(`Belt length L (mm)` = 3, `Arc of contact (deg)` = 0.5, `Belt speed (m/s)` = 0.05),
  hints = c(`Belt length L (mm)` = "L = 2C + (pi/2)(D1 + D2) + (D2 - D1)^2 / (4C).",
            `Arc of contact (deg)` = "theta = 180 - 2 asin((D2 - D1) / (2C)), with the arcsine in degrees.",
            `Belt speed (m/s)` = "v = pi D n / 60 000 using the SMALLER pulley's diameter and speed."),
  digits = 0,
  answers = list(
    tryit_answer("Number of drives whose arc of contact is below the 120 degree minimum", bd_n_fail, tol = 0.01, digits = 0,
                 hint = "Compare each arc of contact with 120 degrees.")
  ),
  intro = "Give belt lengths to the nearest millimetre, the arc to one decimal and speeds to two decimals.",
  question = paste0(
    "<p>Open belt drives: fan drive (D1 = 90 mm, D2 = 280 mm, C = 450 mm, 1440 rpm), pump drive (125, 315, 600 mm, 1750 rpm), ",
    "compact drive (63, 400, 300 mm, 960 rpm). L = 2C + (pi/2)(D1 + D2) + (D2 - D1)&sup2; / (4C); arc of contact on the small pulley = ",
    "180 - 2 asin((D2 - D1) / (2C)) in degrees; belt speed v = pi D1 n1 / 60 000 in m/s. The arc of contact should be at least 120 degrees.</p>")
)
```

<details class="tryit-solution">
<summary>Show the worked solution</summary>

```{r tryit-belt-solution, echo=FALSE}
knitr::kable(bd, digits = c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 2), align = "c")
```

The compact drive's large pulley ratio at a short center distance leaves only `r sprintf("%.0f", bd[["Arc of contact (deg)"]][3])` degrees of wrap: below 120, so it needs a longer center distance or an idler. All three belt speeds are below the 15 to 25 m/s optimum for V-belts, so speed is not the limiting check here.

</details>

### Tension in the belt {#sec-tryit-belt-tension}

A flat belt transmits $3.0$ kW at a belt speed of $14$ m/s over an arc of contact of $150^\circ$, with a friction coefficient $\mu = 0.30$.

```{r tryit-belt-number, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
bt <- list(P = 3000, v = 14, mu = 0.30, theta = 150 * pi / 180)
bt$dT    <- bt$P / bt$v
bt$ratio <- exp(bt$mu * bt$theta)
bt$T2    <- bt$dT / (bt$ratio - 1)
bt$T1    <- bt$T2 * bt$ratio

tryit_number(
  id = "belt-tension",
  title = "Tight-side and slack-side tension",
  answers = list(
    tryit_answer("Net tension T1 - T2", bt$dT, tol = 1, suffix = "N",
                 hint = "P = (T1 - T2) x v, so T1 - T2 = P / v."),
    tryit_answer("Tension ratio T1 / T2", bt$ratio, tol = 0.01,
                 hint = "e^(mu x theta), with theta in radians (150 degrees = 2.618 rad)."),
    tryit_answer("Slack-side tension T2", bt$T2, tol = 1, suffix = "N",
                 hint = "T2 = (T1 - T2) / (ratio - 1)."),
    tryit_answer("Tight-side tension T1", bt$T1, tol = 1, suffix = "N",
                 hint = "T1 = T2 x ratio.")
  ),
  intro = "Work in newtons and radians.",
  question = paste0(
    "<p>A flat belt transmits 3.0 kW at a belt speed of 14 m/s. The arc of contact is 150 degrees and the friction coefficient between belt ",
    "and pulley is 0.30. P = (T1 - T2) v and T1 / T2 = e^(mu theta) with theta in radians.</p>")
)
```

<details class="tryit-solution">
<summary>Show the worked solution</summary>

$$T_1 - T_2 = \frac{3000}{14} = `r sprintf("%.1f", bt$dT)` \text{ N}, \qquad \frac{T_1}{T_2} = e^{0.30 \times 2.618} = `r sprintf("%.3f", bt$ratio)`$$

$$T_2 = \frac{`r sprintf("%.1f", bt$dT)`}{`r sprintf("%.3f", bt$ratio)` - 1} = `r sprintf("%.1f", bt$T2)` \text{ N}, \qquad T_1 = `r sprintf("%.1f", bt$T1)` \text{ N}$$

</details>

## Practice Problems {#sec-belt-problems}

**Problem 1:** A 2 HP motor runs at 1725 rpm and drives a fan through a V-belt drive. The fan must rotate at approximately 860 rpm. If the driver pulley is 4 inches in diameter, what size driven pulley is needed?

<details>
<summary>**Click for answer**</summary>

Required speed ratio: $i = 1725/860 = 2.0$

Driven pulley diameter: $D_2 = D_1 \times i = 4 \times 2.0 = 8$ inches

Select nearest standard size: **8 inch pulley**

Actual output speed: $1725/2 = 862.5$ rpm ✓

</details>

**Problem 2:** Calculate the belt pitch length for a drive with 80 mm and 200 mm pulleys at a center distance of 400 mm.

<details>
<summary>**Click for answer**</summary>

$$L = 2C + \frac{\pi}{2}(D_1 + D_2) + \frac{(D_2 - D_1)^2}{4C}$$

$$L = 2(400) + \frac{\pi}{2}(80 + 200) + \frac{(200 - 80)^2}{4(400)}$$

$$L = 800 + 439.8 + 9.0 = 1248.8 \text{ mm}$$

Select belt length: **approximately 1250 mm**

</details>

**Problem 3:** A timing belt drive has a 20-tooth driver pulley and a 60-tooth driven pulley. If the motor speed is 1800 rpm, what is the output speed?

<details>
<summary>**Click for answer**</summary>

For timing belts, the speed ratio equals the tooth count ratio:

$$n_2 = n_1 \times \frac{Z_1}{Z_2} = 1800 \times \frac{20}{60} = 600 \text{ rpm}$$

</details>
